subject: Client education
label: DESIGN FEEDBACK
caption_ig:
Stop wasting budget on five rounds of website revisions. When you review your next draft, don't play designer—play customer. Describe where a buyer gets confused or distracted, and let your designer build the fix.

#webdesign #smallbusinessowner #websitetips #cro #conversionrateoptimization #designfeedback
caption_fb:
One of the quickest ways a website project goes over budget is vague feedback. Telling a designer to make something 'pop' or look 'more modern' forces them to guess what you mean, leading to endless rounds of edits.

Next time you review site mockups, focus on user friction. Instead of saying you dislike a layout, point out where a customer might miss your main offer or get confused about what to click next. Giving clear, problem-based feedback keeps your launch on schedule.
caption_li:
Subjective feedback is the primary cause of delayed website launches.

When business owners ask designers for 'cleaner' or 'more dynamic' pages, it creates misalignment because aesthetic terms are entirely subjective.

A far more effective framework is pointing out user friction:

• Instead of 'This section is too empty' → 'Buyers might miss our main offer.'
• Instead of 'I don't like this layout' → 'A visitor won't know where to click next.'

When you define the business problem, your designer can create a structural solution without guessing.

How does your team structure design reviews to keep projects moving?

slides.title: Saying 'make it pop' costs you money
slides.body: Vague terms like 'clean', 'pop', or 'modern' force your designer to guess. Every wrong guess adds another revision cycle, pushing back your launch date and burning your budget on endless redesigns.

slides.title: Swap visual preference for conversion risk
slides.body:
Don't say: 'This section feels too empty.'
Say: 'First-time visitors will miss our primary offer here.'
Highlighting revenue risk forces your designer to solve a business problem, not just rearrange white space.

slides.title: Flag user confusion instead of personal taste
slides.body:
Don't say: 'I don't like this layout.'
Say: 'Mobile readers won't know which button to tap next.'
When you describe where a buyer gets stuck, your designer can fix the user flow immediately.

slides.title: Describe the friction, don't prescribe the fix
slides.body: Asking to 'make the button bigger' usually masks the real issue: your headline isn't clear. State the user's goal, point out where they stop, and let the designer handle the layout.
